paragraphs: This paper asks whether a GPT trained to predict the next token also learns something about the underlying world that produces those tokens. The authors derive a causal interpretation of attention and use it to describe a possible internal world model. They also propose extracting causal structure from input sequences at inference time, without task-specific training, and introduce a confidence score for that extraction.

The experiments use Othello and Chess as controlled environments where the legality of a next move can be assessed. Training games came from players trying to win, whereas the test sequences consisted of randomly selected legal moves. This creates a distribution shift while preserving the rules governing valid game states.

The model was likely to produce legal next moves when its attention encoded a causal structure with high confidence. When it generated illegal moves, it also failed to capture that structure. These findings connect the proposed attention interpretation to observed behavior in the tested games, supporting the investigation of causal world models within next-token prediction.
icml-2025-a-causal-world-model-underlyin.tldr: In controlled game environments, GPT’s ability to generate legal moves is associated with confidently encoded causal structure in attention.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression searches for mathematical expressions that describe relationships in data. Its appeal is that the resulting expressions can be compact and interpretable. However, when a dataset has many input variables, searching through possible formulas becomes slow and can produce unnecessarily complicated expressions. Measurement error makes this setting particularly challenging.

The paper introduces PAN+SR, which screens the input variables before symbolic regression searches for an expression. Its variable-selection approach is nonparametric, avoiding dependence on a predetermined functional form during screening. The method combines this idea with a parametric-assisted nonparametric strategy. Reducing the input space is intended to make the subsequent formula search more manageable while retaining predictive accuracy.

The authors also extend SRBench with high-dimensional regression problems covering different signal-to-noise ratios. Across these evaluations, PAN+SR improves the performance of 19 symbolic regression methods, with several reaching state-of-the-art results on the challenging datasets. The contribution therefore concerns a reusable preparation step that can improve multiple expression-search methods, rather than requiring a completely new symbolic regression system.
icml-2025-ab-initio-nonparametric-variab.tldr: PAN+SR screens large input spaces before symbolic regression, improving the tested methods’ ability to discover accurate expressions.

paragraphs: Imitation learning becomes difficult when the learner cannot perform every action available to the expert. The paper formalizes this situation as Action-Constrained Imitation Learning. Because the learner has a smaller action space, it cannot exactly reproduce the expert’s pattern of visited states and actions. This creates a mismatch that ordinary imitation objectives must contend with.

The proposed method, DTWIL, builds replacement demonstrations that obey the learner’s action constraints while following state trajectories similar to the expert’s. It treats the construction of these trajectories as a planning problem and solves it using Model Predictive Control. Dynamic Time Warping supplies the alignment distance, allowing the comparison to accommodate differences in how trajectories progress over time.

The learner then trains on the feasible replacement dataset. Experiments across several robot control tasks show improved performance and greater sample efficiency than the benchmark imitation methods considered. The central idea is to adapt the demonstrations to the learner’s capabilities, preserving useful trajectory information even when the original expert actions are unavailable.
icml-2025-action-constrained-imitation-l.tldr: DTWIL converts expert demonstrations into similar, feasible trajectories so action-constrained learners can imitate more effectively.

paragraphs: Visualizing embeddings from multiple modalities requires deciding what a useful map should preserve. The paper argues that conventional dimensionality reduction methods, including PCA and t-SNE, primarily emphasize feature distributions within individual modalities. This can leave out cross-modal measurements, such as scores describing the relationship between text and images.

AKRMap learns a projection specifically guided by these measurements. After projecting the embeddings, it uses kernel regression to estimate how the chosen metric varies across the map. A regression loss guides the projection network, while adaptive kernels are optimized together with that network. Consequently, the arrangement of points is trained to support an accurate representation of the metric landscape.

The framework also supports zooming and overlays for interactive exploration. Quantitative experiments report more accurate and trustworthy visualizations than existing dimensionality reduction methods, and examples demonstrate comparisons of text-to-image embeddings. Here, trustworthiness concerns how faithfully the visualization represents the cross-modal metric being studied, giving users a map oriented toward a particular relationship they want to inspect.
icml-2025-akrmap-adaptive-kernel-regress.tldr: AKRMap jointly learns projections and adaptive kernels to visualize cross-modal metric landscapes more accurately.

paragraphs: Inverse protein folding seeks an amino acid sequence compatible with a target structure. The paper addresses two difficult settings: complexes containing non-protein components and complexes that occupy multiple structural states. Both require sequence design to account for structural context beyond a single protein configuration.

ADFLIP uses discrete flow matching to generate sequences conditioned on all-atom structures. As generation proceeds, predicted amino acid side chains become additional structural context. For dynamic complexes, ensemble sampling incorporates multiple structural states into the design process. The framework also supports training-free classifier guidance, allowing pretrained models to steer sampling toward desired protein properties without an additional training step for that guidance.

The evaluations include complexes containing small-molecule ligands, nucleotides, or metal ions, as well as dynamic complexes with structural ensembles determined by NMR. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on both single-structure and multi-structure inverse folding tasks. These results support the value of combining detailed atomic context, multiple conformations, and property-directed sampling in a unified protein sequence design framework.
icml-2025-all-atom-inverse-protein-foldi.tldr: ADFLIP designs protein sequences using all-atom context, multiple structural states, and optional pretrained-model guidance.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the initial scale of a language model’s parameters influences what it learns during training. The authors find that smaller initialization scales encourage a preference for reasoning tasks, while larger scales encourage a preference for memorization tasks. The finding concerns a learning bias associated with initialization, rather than a guarantee that a particular scale produces reasoning.

To investigate the effect, the study combines real datasets with carefully designed anchor functions. These complementary settings support examining the observed task preference and its connection to early training behavior. The analysis identifies the embedding space and self-attention mechanisms as particularly important components in shaping that behavior.

The authors develop a theoretical account based on training dynamics and report supporting experiments on real-world language tasks. Together, the analysis and experiments suggest that initialization is a consequential choice for the kinds of capabilities training favors. The practical implication is that parameter scale at the start of training can help guide model development when reasoning performance is a priority.
icml-2025-an-analysis-for-reasoning-bias.tldr: The study links smaller parameter initialization to a reasoning-oriented learning bias and larger initialization to a memorization-oriented bias.

paragraphs: The paper considers stochastic optimization problems whose objectives are differences of convex functions, may be nonsmooth, and depend on a changing data distribution. Its online algorithm uses only observations generated by the current distribution at each iteration. This directly addresses a setting where the source of training samples evolves during optimization.

The algorithm adapts sampling separately for the convex and concave components of the objective. Theoretical analysis motivates these distinct sampling rates. Under suitable conditions on how the distributions converge, the authors prove almost-sure subsequential convergence to DC critical points. This is a conditional result about a subsequence of iterates reaching a form of criticality, rather than a claim of global optimization.

A key technical result bounds pointwise error in sample-based approximations of subdifferential mappings at roughly the square root of dimension divided by sample size, up to logarithmic factors. The resulting sample requirements match specified static-distribution settings with stronger regularity or selection assumptions. Numerical experiments additionally support the algorithm’s efficiency and effectiveness on stochastic nonsmooth problems.
icml-2025-an-online-adaptive-sampling-al.tldr: Separate adaptive sampling rates support conditional convergence guarantees for nonsmooth difference-of-convex optimization under changing distributions.

paragraphs: Contextual bandit algorithms choose actions using contextual information and learn from the rewards they receive. Many analyses depend strongly on a fixed worst-case reward range. That dependence can be unfavorable when occasional extreme rewards make the range much larger than the variance, motivating the paper’s use of robust statistical estimation.

The authors build their approach around Catoni’s estimator and allow general function approximation. When each round’s reward variance is known, variance-weighted regression yields a regret bound whose reward-scale dependence is governed by cumulative variance, with only logarithmic dependence on the reward range. This makes variance a more central quantity in the performance guarantee.

For unknown variances, a peeling-based algorithm avoids an explicit, cumbersome variance-estimation procedure. Its bound retains logarithmic reward-range dependence but introduces additional dependence on the fourth moment. A matching lower bound establishes optimality of the leading-order term. The two results therefore distinguish what can be guaranteed with known variance from what requires additional moment dependence when variance is unavailable.
icml-2025-catoni-contextual-bandits-are-.tldr: Catoni-based contextual bandit algorithms obtain variance-sensitive regret guarantees with only logarithmic dependence on reward range.

paragraphs: The paper introduces emotional face-to-speech: generating speech whose vocal style reflects expressive facial cues. Earlier face-to-speech approaches can capture aspects of identity but struggle with emotional variety. The proposed task makes facial emotion an explicit part of speech generation, with potential applications including virtual character dubbing and support for people with expressive language disorders.

DEmoFace combines a discrete diffusion transformer with a neural audio codec that represents speech at multiple levels. Its multimodal transformer blocks align text and speech while conditioning vocal style on facial emotion and identity. A coarse-to-fine learning curriculum processes the audio token levels progressively to improve training efficiency and generation quality.

An enhanced predictor-free guidance mechanism supports different combinations of conditioning information and helps separate intertwined attributes. Experiments report more natural and consistent speech than the evaluated baselines, including speech-driven methods. The contribution is a coordinated generation framework in which speech content, identity, and emotional expression can all influence the output, rather than leaving vocal emotion implicit.
icml-2025-emotional-face-to-speech-2844a.tldr: DEmoFace uses facial emotion and identity cues to generate expressive speech with a discrete diffusion transformer.

paragraphs: Coordinating several language models can improve reasoning, but exchanging messages between them can be computationally expensive. The paper treats coordination as a game with incomplete information. Each model holds probabilistic beliefs about the others’ strategies and selects a response accordingly, with Bayesian Nash equilibrium serving as the coordination objective.

The proposed ECON framework uses hierarchical reinforcement learning to combine independent reasoning with a centralized final output. Each model chooses responses to maximize expected reward given its beliefs about its peers. This design removes the need for costly exchanges between agents during that response-selection process, making beliefs about other models central to coordination.

The authors prove a tighter regret bound than for the non-equilibrium multi-agent schemes considered. Across six reasoning and planning benchmarks, ECON reports an average improvement of 11.2% over existing multi-LLM approaches. Further experiments incorporate additional models, supporting the framework’s scalability. The contribution joins a game-theoretic coordination objective with empirical evidence that useful collaboration can occur without extensive direct debate.
icml-2025-from-debate-to-equilibrium-bel.tldr: ECON coordinates language models through beliefs about one another’s strategies, improving tested reasoning performance without costly inter-agent exchanges.

paragraphs: Incremental medical object detection requires models to keep learning detection tasks while retaining earlier knowledge. The paper identifies challenges in adapting prompt-based continual learning from classification: foreground and background information are tightly coupled, and prompts interact with image-text tokens through coupled attention. Differences between medical and natural imagery make this transfer especially difficult.

iDPA addresses these issues with two components. Instance-level Prompt Generation extracts fine-grained knowledge about individual objects and creates prompts suited to dense prediction. Decoupled Prompt Attention changes how prompt information enters the model, supporting more direct transfer while reducing memory use and mitigating catastrophic forgetting, the loss of previously learned capabilities.

The authors assemble ODinM-13 from 13 clinical datasets spanning modalities, organs, and categories. They report improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods in full-data and 1-shot, 10-shot, and 50-shot settings. These evaluations support the usefulness of designing prompts around individual detection instances and revising their attention interactions when extending pretrained models to incremental medical detection.
icml-2025-idpa-instance-decoupled-prompt.tldr: iDPA combines instance-focused prompts with decoupled attention to improve incremental medical object detection and mitigate forgetting.

paragraphs: Large Neighborhood Search tackles large mixed integer linear programming problems by choosing neighborhoods in which to search for improved solutions. Those choices strongly affect performance. The paper targets the difficulty of designing effective neighborhood-selection strategies when expert-crafted methods or computationally expensive machine learning approaches struggle to scale.

LLM-LNS uses a language-model agent with two interacting evolutionary layers. The inner layer evolves heuristic strategies to support convergence, while the outer layer evolves the prompts directing that process to maintain diversity. The authors report discovering effective strategies from limited small-scale training data that transfer well to larger optimization problems.

Experiments compare both the strategy-generating agent and the complete optimization framework with existing approaches. The agent outperforms FunSearch and EOH, while the full framework surpasses the evaluated manual and learned LNS methods, Gurobi and SCIP, and additional machine learning optimization frameworks. These are empirical comparisons in the reported evaluations. The broader contribution is an automated strategy-design process that uses language models to guide a consequential choice within optimization search.
icml-2025-large-language-model-driven-la.tldr: LLM-LNS evolves neighborhood-selection heuristics and their guiding prompts to improve large-scale mixed integer optimization.

paragraphs: Building an effective multi-agent language-model system often requires manual configuration or repeated calls to advanced models. The paper reframes that design process as a generation task: given a user query, a model produces a corresponding multi-agent system. This makes adapting the system to the query part of the learned behavior.

The authors represent multi-agent systems as executable code and construct training pairs linking queries to coherent, consistent systems. They use this dataset to train MAS-GPT, an open-source medium-sized language model. A single inference generates a query-adapted system, which can then run to process the query. The single-inference claim concerns generating the system, rather than the entirety of its subsequent execution.

Experiments cover nine benchmarks and five language models, comparing MAS-GPT with more than ten baseline multi-agent methods. The authors report consistent advantages across diverse settings, supporting effectiveness, efficiency, and generalization. The approach makes system construction itself a reusable learned capability, reducing the need to redesign agent configurations manually for each query.
icml-2025-mas-gpt-training-llms-to-build.tldr: MAS-GPT generates executable, query-adapted multi-agent systems in a single model inference.

paragraphs: Molecular prediction tasks often have limited labeled data because annotation is costly. Pretrained graph neural networks offer reusable molecular representations, but those representations still need to be adapted to a particular prediction task. The paper addresses this adaptation step with Multilevel Informed Prompt-Tuning, or MIPT.

MIPT introduces a lightweight prompt-learning module that captures task-specific information at both node and whole-graph levels. This lets adaptation account for local molecular information and the representation of the molecule as a whole. A separate noise penalty targets mismatches between pretrained representations and downstream requirements, reducing information that is irrelevant or noisy for the task.

The experiments report improvements over all evaluated baselines on molecule-related tasks. The authors interpret the results as evidence that MIPT better aligns graph representations with task requirements, while supporting scalable and versatile adaptation. Its central contribution is to combine multilevel task conditioning with explicit suppression of distracting representation content, addressing both what the pretrained model should emphasize and what it should discount.
icml-2025-mipt-multilevel-informed-promp.tldr: MIPT adapts pretrained molecular graph models using multilevel prompts and a penalty for task-irrelevant information.

paragraphs: The paper studies how multiple agents can identify their best actions when groups of agents share the same underlying bandit problem. There are N agents, M clusters, and K possible actions per problem, but cluster membership is initially unknown. The objective is reliable identification with low sampling and communication costs.

Two algorithms organize the work differently. Cl-BAI first groups agents by the bandit problems they face and then identifies each group’s best action. BAI-Cl identifies best actions before clustering agents accordingly. Both use successive elimination, progressively discarding candidates, and receive guarantees that the required identification succeeds with probability at least one minus delta.

The analysis provides sample-complexity bounds and a lower bound for this problem class. When the number of clusters is a small constant, a variant of BAI-Cl achieves order-wise minimax-optimal sample complexity. Experiments on synthetic data, Movie Lens, and Yelp support sampling and communication advantages, especially when clusters are far fewer than agents. That condition highlights when shared structure offers substantial opportunities for cooperation.
icml-2025-near-optimal-best-arm-identifi.tldr: Two algorithms exploit unknown agent clusters to identify best actions efficiently, with conditional near-optimal sampling guarantees.

paragraphs: A time series can become more or less uncertain as its underlying conditions change. The paper argues that diffusion forecasting approaches based on a constant-variance additive noise model can struggle to represent this behavior. It proposes modeling changing uncertainty explicitly as part of probabilistic forecasting.

Non-stationary Diffusion, or NsDiff, uses a location-scale noise model that relaxes the fixed-uncertainty assumption. It combines a conditional diffusion generator with pretrained estimators of conditional mean and variance. These estimates support an adaptive endpoint distribution, allowing the diffusion framework to incorporate information about both the expected value and the uncertainty associated with the data.

NsDiff also introduces an uncertainty-aware noise schedule that adjusts noise levels and incorporates time-varying variances into the diffusion process. Across nine real-world and synthetic datasets, the authors report superior performance over existing approaches. The contribution connects uncertainty estimation to multiple parts of generation, so changing variability influences the forecast distribution rather than being represented through a single fixed noise scale.
icml-2025-non-stationary-diffusion-for-p.tldr: NsDiff incorporates time-varying uncertainty into diffusion forecasting through adaptive distributions and uncertainty-aware noise scheduling.

paragraphs: OmniBal addresses uneven computational work during large-scale distributed instruction tuning of vision-language models. The visual and language components differ in architecture and data distribution, so spreading training across devices can leave some with substantially more work than others. The paper identifies this imbalance in training that uses three-dimensional parallelism.

The framework coordinates changes to data, model partitioning, and memory use. It regroups examples into balanced mini-batches both within devices and across them. A search procedure finds more balanced model partitions. It also adjusts recomputation separately for each partition, using the available memory more fully. These choices are treated as connected because the work assigned to a device and its memory requirements affect one another.

Compared with the open-source InternVL-Chat training code, the authors report roughly a 1.8-fold speedup. Additional experiments across models and datasets support the method’s broader applicability. The result emphasizes coordinated workload balancing as a way to shorten training, with improvements coming from how existing computation is organized across the distributed system.
icml-2025-omnibal-towards-fast-instructi.tldr: OmniBal jointly balances data, model partitions, and memory use to accelerate distributed vision-language instruction tuning.

paragraphs: Cross-domain few-shot learning transfers knowledge from a well-supplied source domain to target domains with few examples. The authors find that training vision transformers with learnable prompts on the source domain can hurt target-domain generalization. Replacing those prompts with random noise, called random registers, consistently improves target performance in their study.

Their analysis suggests that learned prompts capture source-domain information and encourage reliance on visual patterns that are irrelevant elsewhere. They connect this overfitting to sharper loss landscapes. Random registers instead perturb attention, functioning as a form of sharpness-aware minimization that helps the model reach flatter minima and improves transferability.

Building on this interpretation, the authors place random registers on semantic regions of image tokens to strengthen useful attention perturbations. This improves the effectiveness and efficiency of the approach. Experiments on four benchmarks support the explanation and report state-of-the-art performance. The paper’s key insight is that the way additional tokens disturb attention can be beneficial for transfer, even when those tokens do not learn source-specific content.
icml-2025-random-registers-for-cross-dom.tldr: Random register tokens perturb vision-transformer attention and improve cross-domain few-shot transfer in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks have shown promise for predicting molecular solvation free energy, but success on similarly distributed training and test data does not establish performance under distribution shifts. The paper focuses on this less-explored setting, where a model must make predictions in environments different from those encountered during training.

RILOOD combines three mechanisms. A mixup-based conditional modeling module brings information from diverse environments together. A multigranularity refinement strategy learns context-aware representations beyond core molecular substructures, aiming to capture interactions at several levels. An invariant learning mechanism then seeks patterns that remain useful across environments and can generalize to unseen ones.

The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods across the distribution shifts evaluated. These results support considering both molecular context and environmental variation when learning predictive relationships. The framework’s contribution is the combination of diverse-environment modeling, richer interaction representations, and an explicit search for stable patterns, all directed toward more robust solvation free energy prediction under changing data conditions.
icml-2025-relational-invariant-learning-.tldr: RILOOD combines environmental diversity, multilevel molecular context, and invariant learning to improve solvation predictions under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether continuity between image patches helps vision transformers transfer to very different domains with little labeled data. The authors disrupt the smooth visual transitions across patch boundaries and observe a substantial performance drop in the source domain, but only a small decrease in downstream target domains.

Their interpretation is that continuity helps the model learn larger spatial patterns, which transfer less readily than smaller patterns under large domain gaps. In the extreme-gap settings discussed, the findings suggest that transferable information may be concentrated in patterns contained within individual patches. This connects an image representation choice to the scale of visual structure the model learns to use.

Based on that interpretation, the authors propose a method that further disrupts token continuity, encouraging less reliance on large patterns and greater reliance on smaller ones. Experiments report reduced domain gaps and improvements over state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution shows how sacrificing a source-domain cue can improve transfer when that cue mainly supports patterns that do not carry well into distant target domains.
icml-2025-revisiting-continuity-of-image.tldr: Disrupting continuity between image patches encourages smaller-scale visual patterns and improves few-shot transfer across large domain gaps.

paragraphs: Language-model reinforcement learning often uses prompts collected in advance and sampled on a fixed schedule. This paper asks whether training can improve by changing which prompts are presented as learning progresses. Its method, eva, uses reward signals to prioritize existing prompts and generate useful new ones during training.

The framework casts training as asymmetric self-play between a creator and a solver. The creator samples and produces prompts; the solver responds to them. This arrangement allows the training material to evolve alongside the model. The method supports both offline and online reinforcement learning and does not require additional human-written prompts for the reported improvements.

On Arena-Hard, eva raises gemma-2-9b-it’s reported win rate from 51.6% to 60.1% with DPO and from 52.6% to 62.4% with RLOO. Ablation studies support the claim that it produces a meaningful learning curriculum. These results indicate that prompt selection and generation can be active components of reinforcement learning, helping determine what the model should practice as its capabilities change.
icml-2025-reward-guided-prompt-evolving-.tldr: eva uses reward-guided creator–solver self-play to evolve training prompts and improve language-model reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Graph clustering groups nodes without requiring cluster labels, using their connections and available attributes. Real-world graphs can be both large and incomplete, with some node attributes missing. CMV-ND addresses these challenges by preparing complementary views of graph structure that existing clustering methods can use.

The method first recursively expands a node’s neighborhood across different hop distances to capture local structural information completely. It then differentiates those neighborhoods so their representations contain no overlapping nodes across hops. This removes redundancy between views of nearby and more distant connections. Combining K differential neighborhood representations with the target node’s features produces K plus one complementary views.

Existing multi-view clustering or deep graph clustering methods operate on the resulting representations. Experiments on six commonly used graph datasets show significant performance improvements across various methods. The contribution therefore lies in how graph information is organized before clustering: preserving the explored neighborhood information while avoiding repeated inclusion of the same nodes at different distances. This makes the preprocessing useful across multiple downstream clustering approaches.
icml-2025-scalable-attribute-missing-gra.tldr: CMV-ND builds nonoverlapping neighborhood views that improve existing clustering methods on graphs with missing attributes.

paragraphs: The paper explores how models specializing in different tasks can learn through interaction. Inspired by social learning, it introduces Socialized Coevolution as a paradigm for improving a collection of models. Its objective includes both developing capabilities for new downstream tasks and improving performance on tasks the models already perform.

The proposed Dynamic Information Socialized Collaboration framework, or DISC, provides a practical mechanism for these interactions. It includes dynamic hierarchical collaboration and dynamic selective collaboration modules. These organize collaboration and make interactions selective, allowing task-specialized models to acquire knowledge through their exchanges. The emphasis is on adapting collaboration among models rather than treating each model’s learning process as isolated.

The paper presents DISC as a way to realize the broader coevolution idea and discusses potential applications, open questions, and future research directions. Its contribution is consequently both a concrete collaboration framework and a research agenda. The central proposition is that interactions across task boundaries can become a source of learning that benefits existing capabilities as well as the acquisition of new ones.
icml-2025-socialized-coevolution-advanci.tldr: DISC implements Socialized Coevolution through dynamic collaboration among models specialized in different downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Influence functions estimate how individual training examples affect a model’s predictions. The paper investigates why these estimates can be unreliable for deep neural networks, especially with noisy training data. Its diagnosis focuses on estimating the resulting change in validation loss, rather than on estimating how model parameters change.

The authors connect influence-estimation error theoretically to validation risk and its sharpness. Sharpness describes how sensitively the validation loss responds to nearby parameter changes. This connection highlights why a good estimate of parameter movement can still lead to an unreliable estimate of its consequences for validation performance. Flatter validation minima become important for accurate influence estimation.

The paper introduces a new influence-function estimation form designed for flat validation minima. Experiments across several tasks report advantages over existing approaches. The contribution shifts attention to the geometry of the validation objective and its role in translating parameter changes into loss changes. That distinction matters because improving one stage of an influence calculation does not necessarily resolve error introduced by the next.
icml-2025-towards-robust-influence-funct.tldr: The paper links unreliable influence estimates to sharp validation loss and proposes an estimator designed for flat validation minima.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples generated against an ensemble can also affect models that were not available during attack construction. This paper develops theoretical tools for understanding that transfer. It defines transferability error, together with measures of ensemble diversity and empirical ensemble complexity, to make the factors behind success or failure more explicit.

The authors decompose transferability error into vulnerability, diversity, and a constant. This relates transfer to how an adversarial example affects the ensemble’s components and how those components differ from one another. They then use information-theoretic tools to derive bounds involving complexity and generalization terms.

The analysis supports three practical guidelines: use more surrogate models, increase their diversity, and reduce their complexity when overfitting occurs. The last recommendation is specifically conditional on overfitting, rather than a blanket preference for simpler models. Experiments involving 54 models support the theoretical framework. The contribution is an early explanatory foundation for ensemble transferability, connecting ensemble construction choices to error quantities that can be studied mathematically.
icml-2025-understanding-model-ensemble-i.tldr: A theoretical analysis connects ensemble attack transferability to vulnerability, diversity, and complexity, with support from experiments involving 54 models.
